questions.q: What is local SEO for restaurants?
questions.a: Local SEO helps your restaurant show up when nearby people search for what you offer, such as "best tacos near me." It covers your Google Business Profile, reviews, listings, website and links from other sites. Done well, it brings more foot traffic, calls and reservations from your area.

questions.q: How do I get my restaurant into the Google Map Pack?
questions.a: Start with a complete, accurate Google Business Profile with the right categories, consistent name, address and phone number, current hours and good photos. Then build a steady flow of recent reviews, reply to them, and earn links from local sites. Proximity to the searcher also matters, so you'll rank best for people close to each location.

questions.q: Do Google reviews affect my restaurant's local ranking?
questions.a: Yes, Google looks at the quality, quantity and recency of your reviews when it ranks businesses in the Map Pack. Google has also said that responding to reviews helps strengthen your local presence. Asking for reviews right after a great meal and replying to both positive and negative ones covers both sides.

questions.q: Does a multi-location restaurant need a separate page for each location?
questions.a: Yes, each location should have its own page, because Google's local algorithm favors pages with clear relevance to a specific area. Link each Google Business Profile to its location page instead of your homepage. Keep the content unique to that location so it can rank for nearby searches.

questions.q: How can I tell if my restaurant's local SEO is working?
questions.a: Your Google Business Profile dashboard is a good start, since it shows how often your listing appears in Search and Maps and what people do next. Map rank tracking tools show where you appear for a keyword across a grid of points around your location. Check them regularly so you can see which changes move your rankings.

questions.q: Is it worth buying backlinks for my restaurant website?
questions.a: It's best to avoid buying backlinks and earn them through local activity instead. Free local directories, pitches to food bloggers and critics, and local media coverage of events or community collaborations all bring natural links. Those links also send real local visitors your way.
